sections.h: Elihu in the book of Job
sections.b: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, "of the clan of Ram," appears without warning after the three friends fall silent (Job 32:1–5). He is young and waited for his elders, but he is angry: at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without answering him. He gives four speeches. The first, to Job, says God speaks through dreams and through pain, and that an angel go-between may plead for the sufferer and find a ransom (Job 33). The second, to "you wise men," argues that God cannot do wrong (Job 34). The third says human goodness and sin cannot help or hurt God, and that empty cries go unanswered (Job 35). The fourth teaches that God rescues the afflicted through their affliction, then rises into a hymn on the storm (Job 36–37). Then the LORD speaks from the storm, and Elihu is never mentioned again.

A later addition: he is missing from the prologue and from the verdict of 42:7–9, his vocabulary differs, and he quotes the dialogue like a reader (Driver and Gray, Pope). A pompous youth the book mocks: his long preface, his "belly" full of "wind," and his claim to perfect knowledge make him comic (Whedbee, Habel). A true forerunner of God: he brings in suffering as discipline and warning (33:14–30; 36:8–15) and the storm (37), and his questions anticipate God's (Hartley, Calvin, many medieval Jewish commentators). A prophet: the Talmud lists him among seven prophets to the nations (Bava Batra 15b). A mediator figure: Christian readers find Christ in the angel go-between and the ransom of 33:23–24.

The Testament of Job, a Jewish work in Greek from about the first century BC or AD, in no Bible today, treats Elihu as the villain of the story: he speaks insolently, inspired by Satan, and when God forgives the three friends, Elihu alone is not forgiven (Testament of Job 41–43). Gregory the Great's Moralia reads him as a figure of proud believers who speak truth arrogantly. Medieval Jewish philosophers such as Gersonides took him far more seriously, as the human speaker closest to the truth about providence.

common: Elihu's speeches are often called the most debated part of Job.
Most readers agree that his idea of suffering as warning and discipline goes beyond the three friends.
uncommon: Some readers think the LORD's question in 38:2, "Who is this...?", is aimed at Elihu rather than Job.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the reader's own voice
claude.body: Elihu says what many readers feel after the debate: someone must defend God better than the friends did. The book gives that impulse its best voice and then lets God speak past it without comment. This overlaps with Carol Newsom's reading of Elihu as a dissenting reader; the stress on the reader's reaction is mine.

sections.b: Before the LORD speaks, the book brings in a fourth speaker, Elihu, who answers both Job and the friends (Job 32–37). He quotes Job's words back to him, insists that God speaks to people through dreams and pain, and ends with a hymn to the God of the storm. Job never replies to him, and the LORD never mentions him. Whether Elihu is the book's forerunner of God, its comic foil, or a later addition shapes how a reader hears the whole book.

The wisdom tradition honored age: the gray-haired have wisdom (Job 12:12), and Eliphaz pointed to old men on his side (Job 15:10). Elihu, the youngest speaker, challenges that rule: it is the spirit within a mortal, the Almighty's breath, that gives understanding, not many years (Job 32:7–9). He invites the "wise men" to judge Job's words with him (Job 34:2–4), points to God as the teacher no one can match (Job 36:22), and ends with a warning to those who are wise in their own eyes (Job 37:24).

Elihu grounds his right to speak in the spirit: "the spirit within a mortal, the Almighty's breath, is what grants understanding" (Job 32:8), "God's spirit made me" (Job 33:4), and the spirit in him presses to be let out (Job 32:18). He also says every living thing depends on that spirit: if God drew his spirit and breath back to himself, all flesh would die (Job 34:14–15; compare Psalm 104:29–30). Readers differ on whether he claims a prophet's gift or simply the breath every human has from God (Genesis 2:7).

Elihu says God speaks "in a dream, a vision by night, at the hour deep sleep falls on mortals," to turn a person back from a deed and shield him from pride (Job 33:15–17). He borrows Eliphaz's words (Job 4:13), but where Eliphaz's vision taught that no mortal is righteous, Elihu's dream is a warning given in time, like Abimelech's (Genesis 20:3–7). The Hebrew of Job 33:16 says God "seals" their correction. The Greek instead has "with such fearful visions he terrified them," and some modern versions blend the two, so that God frightens people by warning them.

sections.h: An angel advocate and the death-dealers (Job 33)
sections.b: Elihu pictures a dying man drawing near "the death-dealers" (Job 33:22), perhaps angels who carry out death, and then an angel, "a go-between, one in a thousand," who speaks up for him so that God says, "Spare him ... I have come upon a ransom" (Job 33:23–24). The Talmud built on this a picture of the heavenly court: even if 999 argue against a person and one for him, he is saved (Shabbat 32a). The Greek translator read it the other way: a thousand angels of death, not one of whom will harm him. In Job 36:14 the Greek again finds angels, where the Hebrew has "shrine men."

Job longed for someone to stand between him and God: an umpire (Job 9:33), a witness in heaven (Job 16:19–21), a redeemer (Job 19:25). Elihu answers that such a figure may come: an angel, a melits ("go-between, interpreter, advocate"), one in a thousand, who pleads for the sufferer and finds a ransom (Job 33:23–24). Jewish readers see an angel advocate; the Targum calls him an advocate among a thousand accusers. Christians have seen Christ, the one mediator who gave himself as a ransom (1 Timothy 2:5–6), and Christian traditions differ over whether angels plead for people at all.

Elihu moves beyond the friends' simple rule that suffering proves sin. Pain is God's second way of speaking: it brings a person to the edge of the Pit so that he will listen, repent and be restored (Job 33:19–30). God "frees the afflicted through their affliction" and "uncovers their ears for discipline" (Job 36:10, 15). Those who listen live out their days in good things; those who refuse perish "without knowledge" (Job 36:11–12). The book lets this teaching stand but does not let it explain Job, whose suffering the prologue says was not sent to correct him (Job 1:8; Job 2:3).

common: Many readers think Elihu's view of suffering as discipline is the strongest human answer in Job.
uncommon: Some think Elihu's view is only the friends' view again, since he still expects the sufferer to confess sin (Job 33:27).

sections.b: Elihu's picture of a rescue from death uses shachat, "the Pit," five times (Job 33:18, 22, 24, 28, 30), and twice speaks of crossing the shelach (Job 33:18; Job 36:12), which may mean perishing by a weapon or crossing a river of the underworld, as in Mesopotamian poems. Against the Pit stands "the light of the living" (Job 33:30; Psalm 56:13).

sections.h: "They condemned God": a correction of the scribes (Job 32:3)
sections.b: Job 32:3 is one of the eighteen tiqqune soferim, "corrections of the scribes," in the rabbinic lists: places where, by tradition, scribes changed a word that seemed to insult God. Every manuscript reads that the friends "declared Job guilty"; the tradition says the original was "declared God guilty," meaning that by failing to answer Job they had in effect condemned God. Scholars debate whether the lists record real changes or are later reflections on daring passages.

sections.h: Two Ketiv and Qere pairs in Elihu (Job 33)
sections.b: In Job 33:19 the written letters say "strife" (riv) in the sick man's bones, while the reading tradition says "multitude" (rov); the KJV follows the reading, most modern versions the writing. In Job 33:28 the written text says "my soul ... my life," so the healed man is still singing, while the reading tradition says "his soul ... his life." The Greek agrees with the written text.

sections.h: Made of clay, sustained by breath, ruled in the storm (Job 33–37)
sections.b: Elihu says he was "nipped off from clay" like Job (Job 33:6), using the verb Akkadian poems use for the gods pinching off clay to make humans, and that God's breath keeps every creature alive (Job 34:14–15). His last speech celebrates God's rule of the weather: drawing up water as rain from his mist (Job 36:27, with 'ed, the "mist" of Genesis 2:6), sending snow and ice, and hammering out the sky like a metal mirror (Job 37:18, from the root of the raqia' of Genesis 1:6–8).

Elihu says God sends the storm clouds "for a rod of punishment, or for his land, or for loyal love" (Job 37:13). The rod and hesed stand together in God's promise to David's line (2 Samuel 7:14–15; Psalm 89:32–33): God may discipline, but his loyal love does not leave. For Elihu the same storm, like the same suffering, can be either.

sections.h: Elihu among the prophets to the nations
sections.b: The Talmud counts seven prophets who prophesied to the nations of the world: Balaam and his father, Job, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, Zophar the Naamathite, and Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite (Bava Batra 15b). Elihu's own claim that the Almighty's breath gives him understanding and that the spirit within him compels him to speak (Job 32:8, 18) is the kind of claim prophets made (Jeremiah 20:9).

sections.h: One of seven prophets to the nations
sections.b: The Talmud names Balaam and his father first in a list of seven non-Israelite prophets, along with Job, his three friends and Elihu (Bava Batra 15b). The list treats the book of Job as a record of prophecy among the nations, with Balaam as its best-known example.

Elihu's second speech defends God's justice from his nature: the God who made the world and keeps every creature breathing cannot be unjust, or the world would fall apart (Job 34:10–15). A ruler who hated justice could not rule (Job 34:17). God plays no favorites between princes and the poor (Job 34:19), sees every step (Job 34:21–22), and needs no trial date (Job 34:23). Elihu agrees here with Bildad (Job 8:3) and echoes Abraham's question (Genesis 18:25).

Elihu insists that God shows no favor to the rich over the poor, "since every one of them is something his hands made" (Job 34:19), that the oppressors' violence makes the poor cry out to him and he hears (Job 34:28), and that he gives justice to the poor (Job 36:6). Yet he also warns that cries for relief alone, without seeking the Maker, can be empty (Job 35:9–13).
sections.refs: Job 34:19; Job 34:28; Job 35:9–13; Job 36:6; Deuteronomy 10:17; Exodus 22:22–23

sections.b: Elihu's last speech pictures God in the storm: thunder from his pavilion of clouds (Job 36:29; compare Psalm 18:11), lightning wrapped in his hands (Job 36:32), and at the end "From the north comes gold; / fearsome splendor rests on God" (Job 37:22). The north was where Ezekiel saw the storm of God's glory approach (Ezekiel 1:4). In the next verse the LORD speaks from the windstorm (Job 38:1).

sections.h: The storm god's voice given to the LORD (Job 37)
sections.b: Ugaritic poems praise Baal, who "gives his voice" in thunder from the clouds and lives on Mount Zaphon in the north. Elihu's hymn uses the same language for the one God: "he thunders with his voice of majesty" (Job 37:4), "From the north comes gold" (Job 37:22). Like Psalm 29, the poem claims the storm for the LORD, not Baal.

sections.h: The road back from the Pit (Job 33)
sections.b: In Elihu's picture, the sick man who is spared confesses in public, "I sinned, I bent what was straight, yet I was not paid what I deserved" (Job 33:27), and God does this "two times, three times over" (Job 33:29). The Talmud draws from this verse and Amos 2:6 that God forgives a repeated sin up to three times (Yoma 86b).

Elihu says the oppressed cry out but no one asks, "Where is God, who made me, who puts songs in the night?" (Job 35:9–10). God does not hear what is hollow, cries for relief made in pride without seeking him (Job 35:12–13). Job himself, who did seek God (Job 23:3), is answered only when God chooses to speak (Job 38:1).

Elihu promises that the restored sufferer will look on God's face with shouts of joy (Job 33:26), yet he ends by saying, "The Almighty we cannot reach" (Job 37:23), echoing Job's own search (Job 23:3, 8–9). A moment later the LORD speaks, and Job will say that his own eye has seen him (Job 42:5).

sections.h: Clay, dreams and the storm god in Elihu's speeches
sections.b: Elihu's speeches share images with older Near Eastern texts. He is "nipped off from clay" (Job 33:6) with the verb used for the making of Enkidu in Gilgamesh and of humankind in Atrahasis. His sufferer brought near death and then rescued resembles the Babylonian poem Ludlul bel nemeqi. His storm hymn uses the Ugaritic language of Baal's thunder and of Zaphon in the north (Job 37:4, 22). In each case the shared images serve a different faith.
